name: Data Analysis, Statistics and Probability

papers.title: Continuous Universal Fake Factors for jet-to-tau background estimation
papers.abstract: We study Continuous Universal Fake Factors (CUFF), a method for estimating backgrounds from jets misidentified as hadronic tau candidates. CUFF combines four reference-region fake factors for each target tau candidate failing Loose identification. Their weights depend on candidate features and target fail-Loose distributions after subtracting simulated contributions from genuine taus and electrons or muons misidentified as tau candidates. We use ATLAS 2015-2016 Open Data with tau candidates matched to jets with $20<p_T^{\rm jet}\leq60$ GeV. In eight mixtures of reference samples with known proportions, predicted total yields for the Medium identification selection differ from data after subtraction by $+0.7\%$ to $+4.3\%$, supporting the combination. In two validation regions, the corresponding differences are $-21.85\%$ and $-45.84\%$, with statistical uncertainties, including training fluctuations, of $1.58\%$ and $6.03\%$ relative to the data references. These discrepancies lie within broad empirical uncertainty ranges from simulation comparisons between regions, widened by limited simulation statistics. For Loose identification, CUFF and the Universal Fake Factor (UFF) method adapted to public data give similar inclusive yields in one validation region, while CUFF agrees more closely with the data reference in the other. CUFF also describes the shapes of several kinematic distributions more accurately than adapted UFF, including that of an observable not used as a model input. Across nine identification thresholds, relative yield differences vary gradually from $-26.4\%$ to $-19.7\%$ and $-50.2\%$ to $-40.6\%$ in the two regions, respectively, demonstrating consistent application of CUFF at continuously variable tau-identification thresholds without retraining.

papers.title: CLEAR: A Contrastive-Masked Foundation Model for BESIII Event Understanding
papers.abstract: The increasing diversity and complexity of decay channels at high energy physics experiments pose a challenge to analysis workflows, which require time-consuming, labor-intensive channel-specific selections and optimization. This motivates the development of foundation models capable of learning a unified representation transferable across different channels. In this paper, we introduce CLEAR (Contrastive Learning for Event Attention-based Representation), a foundation model designed for physics analysis at BESIII that combines masked modeling and contrastive learning to support decay channel classification and anomaly detection. Masked modeling trains the encoder to predict masked particle features by learning inter-particle correlations, while contrastive learning improves the local clusterability and linear separability of the representation space for discrimination. By further examining the balance between alignment and uniformity, we investigate how contrastive learning shapes the local neighborhood geometry of the representation space and how this geometry relates to classification and anomaly detection performance. Decay channel classification favors a balance between alignment and uniformity, whereas anomaly detection benefits from a greater relative weight on uniformity. For exclusive final-state identification, CLEAR achieves higher signal efficiency than conventional cut-based methods at matched purity and provides a framework that can potentially be extended to other high-energy physics experiments.

papers.title: Using waveform types, discrete Sobolev distances, and trend compatibility to cluster short time series of clinical data
papers.abstract: Clinical tests, such as the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), perturb a physiological system at rest and record its excursion over a fixed protocol window as a short, undersampled time series. Such curves rarely allow parameter identification at the individual level, yet their trends carry physiological information that emerges at the population level as recurrent response patterns. Standard clustering methods aggregate differences globally and average out those trends, losing precisely the information about how the system regains control after the perturbation; identifying response patterns requires a method that preserves them. We present a nonparametric framework that factorizes each curve into unit waveforms, sorts them with a symbolic trend-compatibility filter, and compares compatible shapes using discrete Sobolev-type distances on finite differences up to order $k$. The number of clusters, i.e., distinct response types, equals the number of realizable trend patterns the cohort populates, validated by resampling. Applied to 1283 five-point OGTTs, the method identifies 7 glycemia and 8 insulinemia types. The count holds across a threefold range of resolution. In benchmarks against six classical clustering methods, ours alone never mixes opposite trends, with comparable reconstruction error and stability. Clinical normality, assessed after clustering, is graded, overlapping, and distributed unevenly across response types ($h=0.14$--$0.48$). Overall, our method distinguishes response types among curves too short for alignment-based methods yet too informative for reduction to summary values. It applies to any protocol recording a system's response to a standardized perturbation on a short grid.

papers.title: MuSTRNG: A Muon-Based Synchronizable True Random Number Generation System
papers.abstract: Cosmic-ray muons provide naturally occurring stochastic events detectable by spatially separated devices, offering a potential physical source for synchronized random-bit generation. This is possible because the same physical muons can be independently detected by both devices and used to derive corresponding random-bit segments. Therefore, identifying common muon events and correctly aligning the event sequences are essential for synchronized random-bit generation. This article presents MuSTRNG, a muon-based synchronizable true random number generation system with two synchronization methods: Tracking--Tracking and Tracking--Nontracking. For Tracking--Tracking synchronization, track-based screening removes events whose reconstructed tracks do not intersect the detector area of the other device; angle-based screening partitions reconstructed directions into angular bins and aligns the event sequences to remove inconsistent pairs; and timestamp-based screening compares higher-order timestamp bits to further suppress residual mismatches. Tracking--Nontracking synchronization applies track-based screening only at the tracking-capable device, followed by timestamp-based screening between the two devices. A prototype with two tracking-capable devices was evaluated. For Tracking--Tracking synchronization, the three-stage process reduced the invalid-event ratio to 0.28% using 15-bit random segments, while the generated bit sequences showed generally favorable results in the applicable NIST SP~800-22 tests. Reprocessing the data without track information from one device provided preliminary support for Tracking--Nontracking synchronization, yielding an invalid-event ratio of 0.30% using 5-bit random segments. These results demonstrate the feasibility of muon-based synchronized random-bit generation under different device configurations, with potential application to secure communications.

papers.title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The look-elsewhere effect (LEE) arises when the location of an effect in parameter space is not specified in advance: scanning many locations inflates the significance of the largest excess, and the local $p$-value must be corrected into a global one. A well-established framework, rooted in the work of Davies and operationalised for particle physics by Gross and Vitells, provides this correction for scans over continuous parameters. Some aspects, however, remain unsettled. The definition of "elsewhere" is ambiguous and ranges from a single distribution to an entire experimental programme. Moreover, the analytical shortcuts of the classical framework do not carry over to searches based on machine learning (ML), which are affected by an implicit post-selection bias that depends on the model's resolution and expressiveness. This review covers the LEE in searches for new physics at colliders, from its statistical foundations to these modern challenges. We discuss the corrections for continuous scans and for multiple discrete tests, illustrated with simple numerical examples, and the interaction between ML and the LEE, which we connect to the broader literature on selective inference. We highlight open problems, including the computational cost of empirical calibration for complex models and the development of analytical shortcuts for ML test statistics, and offer recommendations for reporting discovery significance in both classical and ML-based searches in particle physics.

papers.title: Floquet Decomposition: Floquet Multipliers and Time-Periodic Modes from Period-Sampled Snapshot Data
papers.abstract: Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) fits one constant linear operator to a sequence of snapshots. When the dynamics, or the view of them, vary periodically, as in a parametrically excited flow or a rotating structure seen in a fixed plane, no such operator exists, and stability is decided by the Floquet multipliers, the eigenvalues of the map over one period. In the paper that introduced DMD, Schmid observed that snapshots sampled at the period of an oscillatory flow would identify the Floquet matrix. We develop that observation into a method and analyze it. The Floquet decomposition (FD) applies DMD to fixed-rate data subsampled once per period; the ensemble Floquet decomposition (EFD) stacks the snapshots of each period into one column, giving one set of multipliers and phase-resolved modes. For linear time-periodic systems both are exact: FD when the measurement at one instant determines the state, EFD when the measurements over one period do---so EFD succeeds with partial measurements. EFD and Hankel (delay-embedded) DMD use the same data matrix with different shifts between columns. With $p$ samples per period, Hankel-DMD returns each Floquet mode as a carrier with sidebands, a comb of $p$-th roots of its multiplier, which the period shift collapses onto the multiplier. The methods are verified against known multipliers; outside their hypotheses, on nonlinear or noisy data, the estimated moduli are biased and are not decay rates. Measurements of velocity, scalars, and acoustic pressure in a swirl-stabilized combustor illustrate the choice of period, rank, and data scaling.
